Though in his conversation with MEE, he did not seem to want the comparison to be made.

UN migration agency warns of more Gaza hypothermia deaths, as Israel bars 100,000 tents from entering territory
The UN migration agency has warned of further deaths from hypothermia in Gaza as Israel continues to heavily restrict the entry of shelter aid into the territory.
Heavy rains swept through the war-torn enclave last week, inundating thousands of makeshift tents where the majority of Gaza's population is sheltering. A nine-month-old baby died from the cold amid the plummeting temperatures.
"Without proper shelter, without critical relief items, then hypothermia deaths will occur," Karl Baker, head of the International Organization for Migration's Gaza programme, said on Tuesday, adding that children were particularly vulnerable, since they lose body heat more quickly. "It's unacceptable to have hypothermia in the modern world."
Baker said that some 100,000 tents were prepositioned outside Gaza, but the Israeli authorities had barred the entry of items which they consider to be "dual use"- predominantly shelter items including tent poles and mobile homes.
Baker described meeting a drenched family sheltering beneath sagging, worn-out tarpaulins. "Gaza is turning into one large IDP camp (internally displaced persons). It ranks as one of the worst I've walked through," he said.
Reporting by Reuters

The British government has unveiled its first set of sanctions against Israeli companies linked to illegal West Bank settlements, after announcing comprehensive sanctions in September.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the sanctions on Tuesday, shortly before tenders for the E1 settlement bloc - which would effectively split the occupied West Bank in two - are scheduled to be allocated by the Israeli government.
The sanctions are targeting eight Israeli construction, property development and architectural business firms.
The UK is also sanctioning Tsav9, an Israeli group involved in stopping aid trucks from entering Gaza, which the United States also sanctioned in 2024.
The Foreign Office described Tsaz9 as "an Israeli activist movement whose stated mission has been to stop humanitarian aid entering the Gaza Strip, and which has organised and carried out blockades of crossings, ports and roads used by humanitarian aid convoys bound for Gaza".
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the north star of this government’s approach.

The government also imposed sanctions on Tzav 9, a group which it said had regularly blocked humanitarian aid trucks delivering food, water and fuel to the Gaza Strip.

This year marked a quarter of a century since the beginning of the “war on terror”, and in that time, the British state has built one of the most extensive counter-extremism systems in the world.
Also this year, Britain produced - for the first time - an official definition of what it calls “anti-Muslim hostility”. It would be easy to treat these as separate stories, one about security and the other about community relations - but a new report from Cage International argues that they are not.
The definition has been shaped so precisely around the security state that, read closely, it functions less as a protection for Muslims than as a protection for the institutions that have spent two decades treating them as suspects.
The key, as the report sets out, lies in a single word that runs through every part of the definition: intent. Anti-Muslim hostility, as the government defines it, means intentionally engaging in criminal acts against Muslims, or stereotyping them “with the intention of encouraging hatred.” It means discrimination where the conduct “is intended to disadvantage Muslims in public and economic life”.
Discrimination rarely announces itself this way. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed nine officials on Saturday, following an investigation into allegations of oil smuggling in the Jurf al-Sakher area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group.
"In light of the investigation's findings," Zaidi "ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary," his military spokesman Sabah al-Numan said, without identifying the suspects.

Trump may not attack Iran as long as it doesn't provoke US, report says
President Donald Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, according to three people familiar with the matter.
Trump has alternated between threats of escalating the war with new strikes and winding down hostilities, and current and former officials say he does not appear to have made up his mind about how to resolve the unpopular conflict, which he launched in February with Israel.
But in meetings with his national security advisers and after a series of intelligence briefings, Trump said he was considering holding off on strikes, said the people, who, like others interviewed for this story, spoke on condition of anonymity.
He has also indicated sympathy for allies in the region who have asked him not to return to a full-fledged war.
"I could end it immediately, but at the request of the nations that I am looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly," Trump told sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday.
Trump's private comments build on public remarks playing down the likelihood of major warfare resuming.
CALLS WITH SAUDI ARABIA AND TURKEY
In phone calls over the past two weeks, Trump asked for opinions from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, who both urged him not to resume attacks on Iran, according to a senior US official and another person familiar with the matter. They said Trump made no commitment either way.
Trump told bin Salman on 31 October that he was planning to attack after the elections, but the crown prince pleaded for him to hold off, arguing that economic sanctions against Iran were working, according to two more people familiar with the discussion.
Saudi Arabia's Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump has spoken with Erdogan three times since
